The shehnai is a South Asian aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.112, similar to the South Indian nadaswaram, and it was once one of the nine instruments of the Mughal court. Its origin is given in two ways: one account has it brought by the Mughal empire, since it is associated with the Mughal court; another has it originating in ancient India, derived from the pungi and adapted for court performance. The name is variously explained by the Persian shah and nai, by the barber (nai) who improved a seven-hole pipe after the emperor Aurangzeb banned the pungi, and by a corruption of sur-nāl. Western India and the Karnataka coast have their own counterparts; players at temples in Goa and the Konkan and on the west coast are called Vajantri, because they were granted land for serving the temple.

Its range is wide, from a low fundamental up to a high, sharp register, and it is very expressive. The double reed gives it a particular vibrating quality that adds a warm, voice-like trait. The flared bell, of metal or of wood, strengthens the resonance, so that the sound has great penetration and projection. Compared with the Western oboe the shehnai is rougher and more forceful; it is close to the nadaswaram, but its sound is brighter and more direct. Its tone is characteristically South Asian, with a nasal quality, rich in feeling and dramatic tension, and it is much used in court ceremony and traditional music.
